zones.label: Column 1
zones.note: Lexical cross-check, after independent scan reading: the supplied *Entry Words Data of Nippojisho*, NINJAL, Hideyuki Ohshima and Taichi Aida, version 202510, licensed CC BY 4.0 (https://www2.ninjal.ac.jp/textdb_dataset/en/nipp/index.html; https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). The scan-based transcription and English notes are this reviewer's work; the index is not a diplomatic authority.

lines.note: Qinxit is equated with coto and described as a musical instrument. This is the full entry anticipated by the Qinxit catchword on f393; the printed lowercase coto is retained.
The instrument is compared to a harpsichord. This is the dictionary's comparison, not a claim that the Japanese instrument has the same construction.
Nixiqino vye means on top of brocade. The Portuguese begins 'on top of rich fabrics', leading to the example of adding flowers to an already splendid surface.
Qinxǒni fanauo ſô describes adding flowers to brocade. The upright Xix. is the citation label; ſô has an upward circumflex, unlike the headword's caron.

runs.text: Couſas riquißimas, ou mui galantes hũas ſobre

lines.note: The translation explains an accumulation of very rich or elegant things, one on another. The tilde in hũas remains over u.
Completes the piling-up image and interprets it as superfluous or excessive adornment. The explanatory i is followed by a comma in the scan.

runs.text: Carta de bom estilo, ou verſos eſcri-

lines.note: This Qinxǒ concerns a well-written letter or verses. The word is estilo, not OCR estllo; the Portuguese escrito is divided across rows.

runs.text: tos que hum louua, ou aleuanta com hõra. Vt,

lines.note: The writing is praised or spoken of with honour. Vt introduces an example of such a letter or poem arriving.
Qinxǒ tǒrai expresses the arrival of an elegant letter or composition. The row ends with car without a visible hyphen; carta continues below.
Ta completes carta, followed by the alternative of elegant verses. The terminal S. is an upright written-usage label. Typeface update: S. is provisionally italicized under the bulk convention.
Coganeno iro gives the literal sense, the colour of gold. A further figurative sense concerning someone's expression follows within the same entry.
The added sense is a cheerful face. Vomoteni begins an example contrasting a person's outward manner with what is inwardly in the heart.
The example describes forming a pleasant outward relationship, then turns to the heart with cocoroni. The paired outward/inward phrases must be read together across these lines.
The Japanese completes the contrast with an inward 'needle' of judging right and wrong. The Portuguese begins by describing a very cheerful exterior; tçucǒ is retained in the printed historical form.

runs.text: to alegre, & apraziuel, mas no coração não he

lines.note: Completes muito and contrasts a pleasant exterior with a heart that is not the same. The sentence continues rather than ending after the apparent description of cheerfulness.

runs.text: aßi, por q̃ conſidera as couſas doutra maneira,

lines.note: The reason for the contrast is that the person considers matters differently inwardly. The abbreviated q̃ and historical doutra remain unexpanded.

runs.text: & da q̃ ẽtẽder a quẽ fala, ou argumẽta cõ elle.

lines.note: The explanation ends by saying that he gives those speaking or arguing with him something to think about. The scan separates q̃ from ẽtẽder; the nasal abbreviations are retained, not expanded or fused.
This homograph is a golden lamp or lampstand. The printed Candieiro is preserved rather than modernized to candeeiro.
Nixiqito nuimono combines brocade and needlework. The Portuguese starts a description of very rich textiles, dividing peças after pe-.

runs.text: ças muito ricas como brocadilho, & baſtidor,

lines.note: The rich fabrics are compared with brocade and embroidery work. The printed baſtidor remains part of the description rather than being replaced by a modern textile classification.
Broslado adds embroidered work as an alternative description. Its historical consonant sequence is retained exactly.

runs.text: Prohibição, ou ley que hum ſe poem a

lines.note: Qinxu denotes a prohibition or rule one imposes on oneself. The continuation specifies abstaining from wine, distinguishing this unmarked -u headword from Qinxǔ above.

runs.text: ſi de não beber vinho. Vt,

lines.note: The rule is not to drink wine; Qinxuuo ſuru gives the corresponding Japanese example. The scan repeats Qinxu with the object particle uo, not the OCR's Qinzuuo.
The example is translated as imposing this rule on oneself. The grave accent in Pòrſe is preserved.
Tçuyoqi yacuſocu explains a strong or firm promise. The Portuguese adjective phrase continues on the next physical line.
This completes the definition as a firm promise. The two long-s forms in promeſſa are retained.

Qinyet is joy, explained by the Japanese verb for rejoicing. The abbreviated u is kept as printed, and S. is the upright written-usage label. Typeface update: S. is provisionally italicized under the bulk convention.
Nixiqino yama presents a mountain as brocade. The Portuguese explains this through a mountain or woodland's autumn appearance rather than a literal fabric covering.

runs.text: que no Outono parece fermoſo, & de varias co

lines.note: The mountain looks beautiful in autumn, with varied colours. The row ends at co without a printed hyphen, even though cores continues below.

runs.text: res em que ſe mudão as folhas. S.

lines.note: Res completes cores, referring to the colours into which the leaves change. The entry closes with the upright written-usage label S. Typeface update: S. is provisionally italicized under the bulk convention.

Qio concerns being or residing in a place; Qiouo ſaru means leaving that place. Only the opening Suu of the Japanese gloss is legible before an opaque ink blot, followed by the original period after the concealed ending. Suu is therefore a visible fragment, not a claim that the full word ends there; no hidden letters are supplied, and the OCR's Suqeta is not accepted.
Completes Apartarſe: departing from the place or lodging. The blot touches lugar, but the surviving ending and phrase support that word; the next Japanese example begins Qiouo xi-.
Muru completes the Japanese xi-muru example for establishing a dwelling. The Portuguese speaks of determining a place such as a hut.
The place is one in which someone may live. This completes the residence sense of Qio before the distinct falsehood entry.
This Qio means falsity or a lie. Qiouo begins an example whose verb, saying or speaking, is on the following row.
Qiouo yǔ means telling lies. A further sense then begins, describing a condition lacking vigour or substance, with como divided after co-.

runs.text: mo ſem vigor, ou ſustancia. Vt,

lines.note: Completes como and introduces Qioxita as the modifier in an example of a debilitated person. The condition described is weakness or emptiness of vitality.
Fito completes Qioxita fito. The Portuguese describes a weakened person and continues the lack-of-vigour explanation below.

The main text finishes the account of lacking inner vigour. At the far right, the separate printed '(do Rey.' completes the next row's capital/court definition; its physical placement is preserved rather than read as part of the weakened-person gloss or moved to another row.
Qiǒ is equated with Miyaco, the principal city or royal court. The displaced 'do Rey.' is printed at the far right of the row above and supplies the end of this definition.
This Qiǒ means a book; Qiǒuo tozzuru is glossed as binding books. The long-o marks are carons, and En- starts the Portuguese binding verb.
Completes Enquadernar liuros, 'bind books'. The row remains a separate continuation rather than being joined to the example above.
Qiǒbaco is a box or chest for books. Its opening Q belongs to the headword despite the generous type spacing.
Itçuuaritaru fô explains a false law or doctrine. Both printed long-o marks are circumflexes; no accent is added to the first o of Qiobô.

runs.text: Qioca. Sannuru natçu. i, Suguixi natçu.

lines.note: The two Japanese paraphrases both refer to the past summer. This unaccented Qioca is distinct from the humorous-verse headword Qiǒca below.
The Portuguese confirms 'last summer', using verão and estio as alternatives. The historical paßado is preserved.
Qiǒca denotes playful or humorous verse, explained by Curui vta. It begins a new entry at the column's left alignment; the definition continues at the top of column 2.
Continues Qiǒca from column 1: verses please through their meaning or subtlety. The damaged ending is ſutileza, not OCR ſutilega.
Cǒbaxicu and amaxi describe fragrance and sweetness. The Portuguese begins a corresponding fragrant-and-tasty gloss, dividing cheirosa after cheiro-.
Completes cheiroſa and adds tasty or pleasant to the taste. S. is the separate upright label for written usage. Typeface update: S. is provisionally italicized under the bulk convention.
This homograph is a fragrant broth or prepared dish, explained by Cǒbaxij atçumono. Iguaria is divided after igua-.
Completes iguaria goſtoſa, a tasty dish. This closes the food sense before the letter-writing homograph below.
Cǒbaxij fuda supplies an honorific image for a letter. The Portuguese explains it as the letter of a person addressed respectfully, not literally a scented food or broth.

runs.text: quẽ ſe fala honrandoa, & louuando o ſeu es-

lines.note: The person is honoured and the letter's style praised. The initial is h in honrandoa, not OCR b; the row ends es-, completing estilo below rather than the OCR's et-.
Tilo completes estilo. The closing upright S. marks the letter expression as written usage. Typeface update: S. is provisionally italicized under the bulk convention.

runs.text: Lugar, ou terra que aos olhosſe re-

lines.note: Qiǒchi concerns the appearance or character of a place as seen by the eye. The Portuguese representa is divided after re-, and the source's tight olhosſe is retained.
The place appears good or bad; the scan prints maa with two a types. Yoi qiǒchigia gives the favourable case, 'it is a good location'.

runs.text: He bõ lugar, ou chão pera fazer caſas, &c.

lines.note: The favourable location is interpreted as good ground for building houses. The abbreviation bõ remains unexpanded.
Cagamino naca means inside a mirror. The mark over u has two strokes forming a caron, not the OCR grave; the Portuguese espelho continues below.
Pelho completes eſpelho, closing the mirror-interior sense. It should not be joined to the next entry about a person's interior.

runs.text: Interior do homem, ou dentro do

lines.note: This entry describes a person's inner being or the inside of the breast. The o mark is an upward circumflex, agreeing with the repeated form below and differing from the mirror entry's caron.
Fitono qiôchǔuo miſucaſu means seeing through or discerning a person's inner thoughts. Peito completes the preceding definition before Vt introduces the example.

runs.text: Ver, & penetrar o interior dalguem: às ve-

lines.note: The translation speaks of seeing and penetrating someone's interior. Às vezes begins a usage qualification and is divided at ve-.

runs.text: zes ſe diz iſto abatendo, ou moſtrando ter

lines.note: Completes vezes and explains that the expression can be used disparagingly. The qualification continues to describe a low opinion of another person.
The speaker may be showing little regard for someone. This completes the social nuance attached to seeing through a person's interior.
Qiǒcot denotes improprieties or unsuitable conduct. The Portuguese adjective desconuenientes is divided after desconue-.

runs.text: nientes, & que carecem de grauidade, & ma-

lines.note: The conduct lacks seriousness and maturity. Ma- begins madureza, so the word on the next row is not an independent reference to hardness.
Dureza completes madureza, maturity. This closes the noun entry before its adjectival form.
Qiǒcotna is the adjectival form, describing frivolous or inappropriate things. The printed final na is part of the Japanese form, not Portuguese material.
Qiǒcotna fito describes a frivolous person. The scan has both the paragraph mark and Qiǒ-, correcting the OCR's missing mark and Quǒ-.
Co completes pouco, followed by the separately printed maduro. The person is described as lacking maturity; the OCR's comaduro fused the continuation with the next word.
Qiǒcotni is the adverb corresponding to the preceding rash or immature behavior. The scan has t followed by n, not the OCR's m; Adu. labels the adverbial form without repeating the definition.

runs.text: Paßos de garganta, ou ſom ſingular

lines.note: Qiocu denotes vocal runs or a distinctive musical sound. The definition continues with the instrument on the next row; the inherited spelling Paßos is retained.
The musical-instrument qualification completes the first sense. A pilcrow introduces Qiocuuo tçu-cuſu, an expression for bringing an art to a skillful execution; the printed division follows tçu-.
This completes tçucuſu and begins the explanation, performing something skillfully and gracefully. The Portuguese word for some is physically divided al-gũa across the next boundary.

runs.text: gũa arte, como de bailar, tanger, de voltear,

lines.note: The arts offered as examples are dancing, playing music, and tumbling or turning. The initial gũa completes algũa, with the printed nasal abbreviation left unexpanded.
Other similar accomplishments finish the skillful-performance sense. The next example starts Qiocu-uo yǔ and retains the compositor's word division rather than being joined onto this row.

runs.text: Dizer graças, ou couſas que cau-

lines.note: Qiocuuo yǔ means saying witty things or things that cause laughter. The printed yǔ has its length mark, and the Portuguese verb is divided cau-ſão.
This short continuation completes cauſão riſo, cause laughter, and closes the humorous-speech example rather than beginning a separate entry.
Qiǒcu is explained by Curǔ inu, a dog that plays or frolics. The example repeats the headword across a line division after Qiǒ-, distinct from the preceding musical Qiocu.
The playing dog goes after a clod of earth; tçuchicure names the clod and vô the pursuit. The Portuguese ending is vai with final i, not the OCR's val.
This finishes the dog example: after the clod of earth. The printed apos is retained without adding a modern accent.
Qiocuchocu contrasts crooked with straight, as the Japanese Magatta and ſuguna also indicate. The tall initial letter of ſuguna is long ſ, and the Portuguese second member continues below.

Direito completes the straight-versus-crooked contrast; Qiocuchocu funmiǒ says that the distinction is clear. The scan repeats an initial Q, not G, and Xix. is a citation label, not part of the Japanese example.

runs.text: O torto, & direito logo ſe ve.

lines.note: The gloss says that crooked and straight are immediately evident, also allowing the sense of wrong and right. The scan separates ſe and ve; no accent is added to the printed ve.

Qiocuchǔ means inside a chamber or cubicle. The final S. is a visibly upright usage label rather than part of the italic Portuguese sentence. Typeface update: S. is provisionally italicized under the bulk convention.
Qiocumo nai begins a reproachful expression for someone's unsatisfactory conduct. The line ends in abbreviated principalmẽ-, with a visible nasal mark over e, not the OCR's principalmi-.

runs.text: te ſe hum queixa dalguem por não lhe fazer o

lines.note: The initial te completes principalmẽte. The gloss describes complaining about someone who has failed to do what was due; hum and dalguem retain the source's spelling.
The explanation concludes with what the other person ought to have done. The example begins Qiocumo nai cotouo ſu-ru, with long ſ in the first part of the divided verb.

runs.text: Fazer couſas que não diueram fazerſe.

lines.note: This completes ſuru and translates the example as doing things that ought not to be done. The printed diueram is preserved rather than modernizing its first vowel.
Qiocurocu denotes a chair. The one-word Portuguese gloss is complete on this physical row, with no missing continuation.
Qiocuxei is paraphrased as a bending or modulating voice, Magaru coye. The Portuguese gives a voice or vocal run, completed by the throat qualification below.
This short line completes the phrase paßo de garganta, a vocal run or modulation, and belongs to Qiocuxei rather than the following entry.

Qiocuxet introduces pleasing things appropriate to each occasion, continued on the next page. The initial is Q, not D; the damaged but visible nasal mark belongs to acõmo-, which continues as dadas, also printed below as the catchword.
